summary.text: Speciation is the formation of new species, a process that has happened repeatedly in the evolutionary history of life on Earth.
Together with changes within species (anagenesis) and the loss of species (extinction), it has shaped existing patterns of biodiversity.
Evolution as a whole has given rise to biodiversity at every level of biological organisation, and all life shares a last universal common ancestor.

facts.label: Technical name
facts.value: Speciation, the formation of new species

facts.label: Repeated event
facts.value: New species have formed again and again in life's history

facts.value: Anagenesis, change within species, and extinction, loss of species

facts.value: Traits are more similar among species with a more recent common ancestor

items.prompt: Which process produces new species, rather than changing an existing species or removing one?

options.label: Speciation
Anagenesis
Extinction
Mutation

items.explain: Speciation is the formation of new species, while anagenesis is change within species and extinction is loss of species.

items.prompt: Biologists want to explain the pattern of living diversity on Earth today. Which combination of processes does the account name?

options.label: Only new species forming again and again over time
Only mutation and the eventual loss of species
New species forming, change within species, and species lost
Only change within species and the sharing of ancestors

items.explain: Existing patterns of biodiversity have been shaped by repeated speciation, anagenesis and extinction.

items.prompt: A student claims evolution explains only the variety among whole species. How far does the diversity it produced extend?

options.label: Only to the level of whole species
Only to animals and plants
Only to the level of DNA
To every level of biological organisation

items.explain: The process of evolution has given rise to biodiversity at every level of biological organisation.

items.prompt: Species X and Y share a very recent common ancestor, while species Z branched off much earlier. Which resemblance would be expected?

options.label: X and Z tend to be more similar, since age brings likeness
X and Y tend to be more similar in form and biochemistry
All three are equally similar, as traits ignore ancestry
Y and Z tend to be more similar than X and Y

items.explain: Morphological and biochemical traits tend to be more similar among species that share a more recent common ancestor.

items.prompt: A lab wants to reconstruct how species are related. Which approach is now more common than comparing body shapes and chemistry?

options.label: Direct comparison of genetic sequences
Counting how many species share a habitat
Comparing only the fossils of each group
Ranking species by how many offspring they have

items.explain: Traits were historically used to reconstruct phylogenetic trees, although direct comparison of genetic sequences is a more common method today.

items.prompt: A child asks whether she and a bacterium on her hand share any ancestor. What would a biologist say?

options.label: No; humans and bacteria began as two separate lines
Only if the bacterium lived in a human body
Yes; all life shares one last universal common ancestor
No; only animals share an ancestor with humans

items.explain: All life on Earth, including humanity, shares a last universal common ancestor.
